title: Prototyping an isometric sci-fi ARPG using GPT-6 Astra and Meshy v7 (Unreal Engine 5.8)
author: freesoulapps
selftext:
Working on an isometric sci-fi ARPG prototype to see how much of a solo workflow can be handled with GPT-6 Astra and generative 3D tools.

**Current setup:**

* **Engine:** Unreal Engine 5.8
* **Characters:** Meshy v7 (multi-view reference images to 3D)
* **Game Logic & Scene:** GPT-6 Astra for outpost layout, voiced NPC dialogue system, and quest tracking

Testing how far this pipeline can go before hitting limits on gameplay complexity and asset consistency.

Curious if anyone else here is using Astra or Meshy for playable ARPG prototypes—what parts of your pipeline are working smoothest, and where are you running into walls?

*(Full video:*[*https://youtu.be/kWqB59MmIfo*](https://youtu.be/kWqB59MmIfo?utm_source=gemini)*)*

comments.author: AshenThroneDev
comments.body:
Meshy has been the smoothest part of our pipeline too. For Ashen Throne we take concept art through Meshy image-to-3D, then render each unit in a fixed headless Blender rig into a sprite atlas for the map. The wall we hit was asset consistency, and what fixed it wasn't better prompts: it was forcing every model through the same camera, lighting and scale in that render step, so a unit made in week one sits next to one made in week ten without looking like it came from a different game.

Where I'd expect Astra to struggle is quest state, not layout. Dialogue and outposts are easy to regenerate, but a quest system that has to survive saves, reloads and a player doing things out of order is where you want hard rules written down and tested, not re-derived every session.

replies.author: freesoulapps
replies.body: Doing the exact same thing with headless Blender—normalizing the render pass is really the only way to keep assets from drifting.

comments.author: Infinite-Switch6948
comments.body:
This little base camp is looking good. What kind of poly counts are you getting with those vehicles? are you doing a retopology pass?   
  
I am working on a Turn Based Dungeon Crawling Roguelike and havn't hit any major snags yet, I've definitely had to scrap entire processes and start over once I realized there was a more efficient or more stylized way to do things. Best thing I have learned so far is to turn any repeatable actions into scripts and just get astra to run the script vs trying to manually do everything in the exact same method. 

For instance the last script I created was a grip script for my character models when fitting all of the game's weapons to the different grip types. Once the weapon is modeled and approved then grip script measures radius of weapon handle, adjusts finger rigs and arm rigs, measures for any clipping or collisions and makes any corrections based on the feedback. Uses very few tokens once the script has been proven.

replies.author: freesoulapps
replies.body:
Astra actually handled the mesh cleanup and optimization pass directly—no manual retopo.
That grip script setup is really smart, by the way. Having Astra trigger proven, deterministic scripts instead of trying to prompt transformations from scratch saves a massive amount of tokens.

comments.author: Eshinio
comments.body: Looks awesome! Would love to hear if you have some tips on how you planned and structured the game with Astra. Did you build like a game manifest with information about all features in the game, and how big "chunks" did you have Astra working on at once? I only got the Plus plan, so I'm worried how much is possible to create before hitting limits...

replies.author: freesoulapps
replies.body:
Honestly didn't start with a big game doc or manifest at all. I just wanted to see how good Astra actually was at turning 2D references into 3D scenes.
​Asked it for 3 isometric ARPG ideas, had it generate reference images for what it envisioned, and then told it to try recreating all 3 scenes in Blender and Unreal. Picked whichever one turned out best visually and kept iterating until it got close to the reference, then brought in the Meshy v7 characters (multi-view to 3D). Once that felt solid, that's when I finally used Astra to map out the bigger game—main story, map zones, character backgrounds, all of that.
​As for limits, I'm on the Pro(X20) plan and get about 2.5 to 3 days of non-stop agent runs before hitting the weekly cap. Because of that, I now offload anything non-visual (story, quest logic, dialogue writing) to Claude, and save Astra strictly for the visual and in-engine passes.

comments.author: Cloudy_Day912
comments.body:
I’ve had better results treating them as different parts of the same workflow. Astra handles the scene planning and logic, then I use Meshy for the base 3D assets, especially when I can provide multiple views.

The real headache starts in Blender/Unreal though. Scale, materials, topology and naming still need cleanup, and some assets have to be regenerated to keep the art style consistent. At that point, workflow consistency and Astra usage can become the bigger bottleneck.
